analysis.one_liner: Eliminates generic drug copays for the lowest-income Medicare prescription drug enrollees.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee with no cosponsors and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend Medicare Part D's low-income subsidy program so that, starting in 2026, enrollees at the lowest income levels pay $0 for generic drugs, instead of the current $1 copay. The small copays on other preferred drugs would be kept but indexed to rise with inflation. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Lowest-income enrollees in Medicare's prescription drug benefit (the Low-Income Subsidy program), who would stop paying the $1 copay for each generic prescription starting in 2026. Removing even a $1 charge is meaningful for this population because small cost-sharing is known to cause some low-income patients to skip or delay filling prescriptions.

how_it_helps.text: Starting in plan year 2026, the copay for generic drugs under Medicare Part D's Low-Income Subsidy drops to $0, eliminating the current $1 charge per generic prescription for the lowest-income enrollees.

Copays on preferred multiple-source drugs (currently $1) and other drugs (currently $3) remain but would be indexed to increase with the consumer price index, preventing erosion of the program's baseline copay structure.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The government covers most cost-sharing for low-income Part D enrollees, so eliminating the generic copay shifts that small cost from individual beneficiaries to the federal Medicare program. To the extent the $0 copay leads to more filled prescriptions, drug makers and Part D plans would fill more low-income prescriptions.

drawbacks.text: The federal government bears the cost of the eliminated copays, a modest but real increase in Medicare spending that grows as drug use rises, since the change takes effect in 2026 with no expiration.

The bill does not address the much larger cost-sharing problems in Part D, such as brand-name drug costs for low-income enrollees or the copays faced by beneficiaries just above the lowest-income threshold, so its direct benefit is narrow.
Indexing the remaining $1 and $3 copays to inflation means those charges slowly rise over time rather than being eliminated or reduced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it removes a $1 copay per generic prescription for the poorest Medicare beneficiaries, a group for whom even small charges measurably reduce prescription filling. The cost to the federal government is small relative to Part D spending overall. The bill leaves most cost-sharing untouched, so it is a targeted improvement rather than a broad fix, and its inflation indexing means the residual copays creep upward over the years.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no committee action and no cosponsors until Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Casey introduced the Cutting Copays Act on March 14, 2024.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, its only action of the entire Congress.
The bill drew zero cosponsors and never received a committee markup or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lowest-income Medicare beneficiaries are no better off, and the federal Medicare program saves the small cost of the eliminated copays. Nothing changed for drug plans, pharmacies, or manufacturers because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: no one's copays changed

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to eliminate generic drug copays for the lowest-income Medicare Part D enrollees and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee where the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action; it received no markup or vote during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator was ever attached to the bill, so no party-line pattern can be read from the record; it simply never attracted support from either party.

industries.note: Plans administer the low-income subsidy cost-sharing and would collect the same federal subsidy payments with one less charge to pass to beneficiaries; the effect on their finances is minor. More filled prescriptions increase dispensing volume.
A $0 copay for generic drugs among the lowest-income enrollees would likely increase generic prescription fills, modestly raising volume for generic manufacturers at no cost to the patient.
The government, which already subsidizes cost-sharing for low-income enrollees, absorbs the eliminated copays as additional Medicare spending.
